title: Korean Media Watchdog Sanctions 11 Shows Over Misleading Health Claims
subtitle: Broadcasters face official warnings for exaggerating dietary supplements as cures for dementia and cancer.
dossier_facts: South Korea's media regulator issued formal cautionary warnings to 11 health-infotainment broadcasts.
Major terrestrial and cable networks including MBC, SBS, JTBC, TV Chosun, Channel A, and tvN were implicated.
The decision targets misleading claims blurring functional dietary supplements with clinical medical treatments.
body_html:
Cracking Down on Wellness Hype

South Korea’s media regulator has stepped in to curb an increasingly pervasive trend across television networks: turning dietary supplements into miraculous cure-alls. In a decisive plenary session held in Seoul, the Korea Communications Standards Commission (KCSC) issued statutory cautionary sanctions against 11 health infotainment programs across major terrestrial and cable channels for broadcasting exaggerated, medically unsubstantiated claims.

The Blurring Line Between Supplements and Medicine

At the center of the controversy were ingredients heavily marketed within Korea's booming inner-beauty and preventative wellness sectors, such as phosphatidylserine, fish scale collagen, and kamut enzyme. While phosphatidylserine is officially certified by Korea’s Ministry of Food and Drug Safety solely for helping improve age-related cognitive decline, eight high-profile shows—including SBS’s Good Morning, MBC’s Health Reconstruction Sherlock, and JTBC’s Rewriting Health Notes—framed it as a definitive preventive measure against dementia. Elsewhere, MBN’s While You Were Sick falsely claimed that fish scale collagen, recognized merely for skin hydration, could thwart cancer recurrence, while tvN’s Choice of 7 Billion mistranslated overseas interviews to aggressively market kamut enzyme for weight loss.

Accountability in a Health-Conscious Society

The regulatory body emphasized that conflating health functional foods with pharmaceutical treatments poses severe public health risks, urging broadcast networks and guest medical experts to exercise strict editorial integrity. Outside the wellness sector, sanctions were also handed to Lotte Home Shopping for likening cosmetic creams to medical dermatology injections, signaling an expansive drive by Korean authorities to hold lifestyle media accountable to international scientific standards.

title: Inside ‘Night in Seoul’: The Cinematic Reckoning of Korea’s Martial Law Crisis
subtitle: Directed by investigative journalists and cinema masters, the documentary turns a fateful night of democratic resistance into high-octane cinema.
dossier_facts: Official Release: Opens nationwide in South Korean theaters on December 3, marking the crisis’s two-year anniversary.
Creative Team: Helmed by directors Cho Chul-young, Kim Shin-wan, and Kim Jong-woo, featuring technical crew from 'Parasite' and '12.12: The Day'.
International Accolades: Awarded the NETPAC Jury Special Mention at the International Film Festival Rotterdam, with screenings at Hot Docs and Udine.
body_html:
The Six Hours That Shook the Peninsula

On the night of December 3, 2024, at 10:28 PM, South Korea paused in disbelief as then-President Yoon Suk Yeol declared emergency martial law. Inside the offices of MBC’s acclaimed investigative program PD Notebook, producers grabbed handheld cameras and rushed toward the National Assembly. What ensued was an astonishing display of civic resolve: lawmakers climbing fences past police barricades, parliamentary aides barricading halls against armed troops, and crowds of citizens assembling under winter skies to defend the perimeter. That pulse-pounding night now arrives on the silver screen in Night in Seoul, an urgent feature documentary co-directed by Cho Chul-young, Kim Shin-wan, and Kim Jong-woo.

Cinema-Grade Craft Meets Generational Memory

Far from a simple compilation of television reporting, Night in Seoul meticulously reimagines the ordeal for the theatrical medium. To recreate the sensory shock of the siege, the directors collaborated with sound and visual artists whose credits include Bong Joon-ho’s Parasite and the smash-hit political thriller 12.12: The Day. From the visceral roar of military transport helicopters to the echoing shouts inside parliamentary corridors, the auditorium becomes an immersive pressure cooker. Crucially, the filmmakers intercut footage of the 2024 standoff with haunting archival moments from the 1980 Gwangju Democratization Movement. Under the guiding narration that 'the dead save the living,' the film underscores how historical scars emboldened everyday citizens and hesitating military personnel to draw the line against authoritarian force.

Global Resonance in an Era of Fragile Democracies

Though deeply anchored in Korean contemporary history, the film has quickly captivated overseas audiences. Premiering internationally at the International Film Festival Rotterdam—where it captured a prestigious NETPAC Jury Special Mention—before making stops at Hot Docs and the Udine Far East Film Festival, foreign viewers have responded to the documentary as an electrifying political thriller. According to director Kim Shin-wan, global audiences intimately connected with the narrative amidst worldwide concerns over political polarization and institutional erosion. Premiering theatrically this December, Night in Seoul stands as a cinematic triumph of resistance, documenting the night South Korea stood up to protect its hard-won democracy.
